claims.text: The starting material is an equimolar HfNbTaTiZr concentrated alloy.
The modeled HfNbTaTiZr is a bulk, defect-free crystal.
The high-temperature comparison material contains 1 wt.% oxygen.
A framework coupling ab initio calculations to machine-learned interatomic potentials can explicitly calculate phonon and electronic thermal conductivity separately.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
The integrated model captures atomic-mass variation, force-constant variation, anharmonicity, and oxygen-impurity effects.
Direct atomistic treatment avoids reliance on empirical parameters such as Debye temperature.
Direct treatment of anharmonic interactions and impurities is sufficient to decouple phonon and electronic transport channels.
The framework will make the separate transport contributions approximately 30% more accurate than earlier estimates.
The framework will reproduce comparable lattice and electronic contributions below 200 K.
For oxygen-doped HfNbTaTiZr, the predicted total conductivity will be 10–17 W/(K m) from 300 to 1200 K.
Earlier approaches generally require Debye-temperature approximations.
Earlier approaches typically conflate lattice and electronic thermal transport.
The predictive capability applies to bulk, defect-free HfNbTaTiZr and oxygen-doped variants under controlled laboratory conditions.
The approach may not apply to specimens with high defect concentrations or non-equilibrium processing histories.
Time-domain thermoreflectance and electrical measurements combined with the Wiedemann–Franz law can separately resolve the lattice and electronic conductivity components in these samples.
Deviation of both separately measured contributions from predictions by more than approximately 30% across the low- and high-temperature regimes would falsify the claimed performance.

contradictions.description: The applicable material is repeatedly described as defect-free while also containing a controlled oxygen impurity whose effects are explicitly modeled. An oxygen-doped crystal is not literally defect-free unless the term is qualified to mean free of defects other than oxygen.

The hypothesis confidently claims accurate decoupling below 200 K, whereas the uncertainty field says decoupling efficacy in that same temperature range requires further empirical validation. This is a tension in confidence rather than a direct numerical contradiction.
